column2: How can successful treatment increase the prevalence of a disease?
column3: Prevalence rises with longer duration, so extending survival raises the number living with the condition without any increase in new disease.

column3: Randomisation averages out both known and unknown confounding, whereas adjustment by design, stratification, regression, or propensity scores can leave unmeasured confounding.

column3: It is the reciprocal of the absolute reduction, and the same relative effect gives a larger absolute reduction when baseline risk is higher.

column3: Overdiagnosis identifies genuine pathology that would never cause symptoms in the person's lifetime, so the abnormality is real and confirmation cannot exclude it.

column3: Raising the threshold improves specificity but misses disease, so the choice weighs the consequences of delayed diagnosis against those of unnecessary follow-up.
